questions.title: Generics — Type Safety and Type Erasure
questions.question: How do Java generics work and what is type erasure?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Generics: compile-time type safety — catch ClassCastException at compile time**
- **Type erasure: generic type information removed at runtime — `List<String>` becomes `List` at runtime**
- **Cannot: `new T[]`, `instanceof T`, `new T()` — erased at runtime**
- **Bounded type parameter: `<T extends Comparable<T>>` restricts what T can be**
- **Red flag:** not knowing that `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same type at runtime

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Generics provide compile-time type safety — instead of casting from `Object` and risking `ClassCastException` at runtime, the compiler verifies types at compile time. `List<String>` guarantees you only add and get `String` objects without explicit casting.

Type erasure is how Java implements generics: at compile time, the compiler checks generic types, then removes (erases) them from the bytecode. `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` both become just `List` at runtime — you can't use `instanceof List<String>` or create `new T[]` because the type parameter is gone.

This is why `List<String>` is not a subtype of `List<Object>` even though `String` is a subtype of `Object` — this would break type safety since you could add an `Integer` to a `List<Object>` reference that points to a `List<String>`.

questions.title: Wildcards — Producer Extends, Consumer Super
questions.question: What is the PECS principle and when do you use upper vs lower bounded wildcards?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super**
- **`? extends T`:** read from it — can be T or any subtype (covariant)
- **`? super T`:** write to it — accepts T and supertypes (contravariant)
- **`?` (unbounded):** either reading as Object or calling method that works on any type
- **Real use: `Collections.copy(dest, src)` — `List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src`**
- **Red flag:** using raw types instead of wildcards — loses type safety

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
PECS stands for Producer Extends, Consumer Super — a mnemonic for choosing between `? extends T` and `? super T`. Use `extends` when the collection produces values you'll read from it; use `super` when the collection consumes values you'll write into it.

`List<? extends Number>` can hold any list of Number subclasses — `List<Integer>`, `List<Double>`. You can read `Number` from it safely. But you can't write to it because you don't know the exact type — is it a `List<Integer>`? A `List<Double>`? The compiler prevents writes.

`List<? super Integer>` can hold any list that's a supertype of Integer — `List<Integer>`, `List<Number>`, `List<Object>`. You can safely write `Integer` to it. But reading gives you `Object` — the compiler only knows the element is at least `Object`.

When in doubt: if you need to do both, use a concrete type parameter `<T extends Number>`.

questions.title: Generic Design Patterns
questions.question: How do you use generics to create reusable, type-safe APIs?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Generic repository/service pattern: avoid code duplication across entity types**
- **Heterogeneous container: use `Class<T>` as key for type-safe containers**
- **Builder with generic SELF type: fluent API that returns concrete subtype**
- **Generic Result/Either type: type-safe error handling without exceptions**
- **Red flag:** copy-pasting the same service code for different entity types — generics solve this

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Generics let you write code once and use it safely with different types. The most common pattern in Spring applications is the generic base service or repository that provides CRUD operations for any entity, avoiding code duplication across dozens of entity types.

Another powerful pattern is the type-safe heterogeneous container — using `Class<T>` as a key in a map so you can store and retrieve instances by their type without casting. Spring's `ApplicationContext.getBean(Class<T>)` uses this pattern.

The generic `Result` type — similar to Rust's `Result<T, E>` or functional languages' `Either` — is increasingly popular: wrap return values to represent success or failure without throwing exceptions, enabling cleaner error handling in functional pipelines.
